sections.title: Start here: the diversified private developer
ps: Invenergy is the second-largest developer in the United States by {{development pipeline}} — 41,328 MW behind NextEra — and it is owned by a Quebec {{pension fund}}, a Blackstone {{infrastructure fund}} and its own managers. It builds wind, solar, batteries, gas plants, an 800-mile HVDC line and a solar-module factory. This guide teaches what that combination is: how one company allocates capital across five technologies, why owning transmission changes what a developer can build, how a private company of that size is owned and financed, and where the model breaks.

**What it deliberately does not repeat:** the Aypa guide teaches the contracted storage platform as an asset a buyer prices; the Spearmint guide teaches the merchant developer and the pre-COD market; the Intersect guide teaches the co-located energy park and who may use a grid connection. The Classroom owns how a battery earns money hour by hour. Here the unit of analysis is the developer's whole capital budget, and storage is one line in it.

**One idea carries the guide.** A diversified developer is a machine for turning permits, land and grid positions into whichever asset the buyers and the policy of the moment will pay for. In 2022 the buyers paid for offshore wind leases; in 2026 they pay for gas plants sold to utilities and for the transmission line that makes new sites possible. The company is the same; the fuel changed.

sections.title: One capital budget, five products
ps: A pure-play storage developer has one question: which battery to build next. A diversified developer has a harder one: which *asset class* earns the best return on the same development capability — the land team, the interconnection engineers, the permitting lawyers, the construction group. Invenergy's five products all use that machine, and each converts it into cash a different way.

**Wind and solar** are the volume business. The developer signs a {{PPA}} or {{virtual PPA}} with a corporate — Meta's 1,800 MW, Verizon's more than 1 GW — or an {{environmental attribute purchase agreement}} that sells the certificates while the electricity goes to the grid, then builds and either holds the plant or does a {{farmdown}}: WEC Energy Group is majority owner of Delilah I and Hardin III with Invenergy as developer and operator. The developer's return is the margin between what the project cost and what a long-term owner pays for contracted cash flow.

**Storage** in Invenergy's record is a utility-contracted Southwest business — eleven Arizona batteries for APS, a solar-plus-storage site for SRP — and a set of large development microsites (Cloud Cap at 1,000 MW / 4,000 MWh, Hazy Peak at 700 MW / 2,800 MWh) with no offtaker yet. It is built on the same land-and-interconnection machine as the wind and solar, and it shows why the machine matters more than the technology: the sites were assembled before the buyer existed.

**Gas** is the growth line of 2025–2026, and it uses a different exit: {{build-own-transfer}}. Indiana Michigan Power filed a {{CPCN}} to buy the 918 MW Sycamore Riverside plant and take ownership in March 2029; We Energies filed to buy two Wisconsin plants for its data-centre load. The developer carries the plant through permitting and construction and sells it into the utility's {{rate base}} at commissioning — the utility's customers pay for it over forty years, and the developer is out at year three.

**Transmission** is the product no other developer in this corpus sells: {{merchant transmission}}. Grain Belt Express earns from transmission service agreements with 39 Missouri municipal utilities under an {{open access transmission tariff}}, not from a regulated rate base. It is also the product that makes the others possible, which is the next section.

**Manufacturing and services** — Illuminate USA's module plant, Invenergy Services' operations arm — capture margin the developer would otherwise pay to suppliers and make the projects eligible for domestic-content bonuses. They are the machine feeding itself.

The allocation rule is visible in one number: the USD 765 million Interior paid in June 2026 to cancel four {{offshore wind lease}}s was committed, in the company's own words, to gas plants in five states and to geothermal. Capital moved from the technology the federal government stopped permitting to the two it will.

sections.title: Why a pension fund and a bank fund own a developer
ps: A developer at Invenergy's scale needs billions of equity it cannot raise from founders, and it will not list — a public developer's share price punishes the lumpy, permit-dependent cash flow of development. The alternative is direct ownership by institutions that price long-dated cash flow: a {{pension fund}} and an {{infrastructure fund}}.

**The pension fund** is the patient owner. CDPQ's liabilities are pensions payable for decades, so it wants assets that pay for decades and does not need to sell. That is why it can hold a majority economic stake since 2018 without an exit plan, and why the company can leave management as {{managing member}}: the fund is buying cash flow, not control.

**The infrastructure fund** is a different animal. Blackstone Infrastructure Partners invests {{limited partner}} money through a {{general partner}} that earns fees and a share of profits; its open-ended structure means it need not sell on a clock, but it must show its investors a return, which is why it wants the platform to keep growing — hence USD 3 billion in 2022 and another USD 1 billion in 2023, and why the pipeline ranking matters to it.

**What the structure buys the developer.** Equity for ten-year projects at a cost no bank would offer; a {{revolving credit facility}} sized on the owners' names (sixteen lenders at USD 1.5 billion); and the standing to be the buyer of other people's portfolios — the Invenergy-led consortium with CDPQ and Blackstone bought AEP's 1,365 MW of unregulated renewables for USD 1.5 billion enterprise value in 2023.

**What it costs.** Two owners with different clocks and a management that controls but does not own most of the economics. Every large decision — an offshore exit, a gas pivot — is a negotiation among three parties whose incentives usually align and occasionally do not. The company publishes none of it; the reader infers it from what gets funded.

sections.title: What owning transmission changes
ps: A developer's scarcest input is a place on the grid where new generation can connect. The {{interconnection queue}} rations it; a {{queue position}} takes years and can fail in the study. A developer that builds its own line creates connection points that did not exist — and decides what plugs into them.

**Merchant HVDC in one paragraph.** Grain Belt Express is 800 miles of 600 kV direct-current line from western Kansas to Indiana with a {{converter station}} at each end of Phase 1 (Siemens Energy), 5,000 MW of capacity and a stated USD 11 billion cost. It is {{merchant transmission}}: its revenue is transmission service sold under a FERC {{open access transmission tariff}} — 39 Missouri municipal utilities are contracted — not a utility's regulated rate base. Its financing is private after the DOE {{loan guarantee}}'s {{conditional commitment}} of USD 4.9 billion was terminated in July 2025.

**What the line buys the developer.** Every generator that connects at the Kansas end is a customer for the line and a project the same developer can build: Energies Media reported in March 2026 that Invenergy's western Kansas wind projects are 'tied to the Grain Belt Express transmission corridor'. The company has also said the line will carry 'coal, gas, and nuclear' — the fuel on the wire is whatever the buyers at the far end want. And a converter station is a siting anchor for a large load: an HVDC terminal delivers gigawatts to one point, which is what a data-centre campus needs.

**What it costs.** A decade and a half of state certificates — Indiana 2013, Kansas and Missouri 2019 amended 2023, Illinois 2023 upheld by the state supreme court in January 2026 — thousands of {{easement}}s (USD 105 million executed, 'over 1,500 voluntary agreements'), {{eminent domain}} petitions against the holdouts, a state attorney general's investigation, and USD 1.7 billion of EPC awards to Quanta and Kiewit made while the federal guarantee was still conditional. The developer that owns the line also owns every one of those fights.

**The comparison.** Intersect's answer to the grid-connection problem was to put generation, storage and the load behind one fence. Invenergy's is to build the wire. Both are ways to stop waiting in a queue; one is measured in fence lines, the other in states.

sections.title: Where it fails
ps: **The line is financed on private capital or not at all.** After the DOE {{loan guarantee}} was withdrawn, Grain Belt Express needs USD 11 billion from banks, bonds and equity partners against transmission service contracts and a state certificate that is still being contested by the Missouri Attorney General. No financing has been announced. If it does not close, USD 1.7 billion of EPC awards and USD 105 million of {{easement}}s are stranded and the Kansas wind projects behind them lose their route to market.

**Policy can refund you and still beat you.** The USD 765 million offshore settlement returned the lease prices, not the development spend on Leading Light Wind, and it came with a condition — 'demonstrating necessary investments in U.S. conventional energy development' — that dictates where the money goes. A developer that takes federal money for exiting one technology is committing itself to another.

**Boilerplate is not a balance sheet.** '36 gigawatts developed' in April, '38' in May; '20 gigawatts operated' then '25'; 'largest privately held' with no ranking behind it. A reader who wants to know what Invenergy owns cannot find out. Every figure in this guide is a transaction someone else announced.

**Build-and-transfer lives or dies at the commission.** The gas plants earn nothing until a {{CPCN}} is granted and the price is approved into {{rate base}}; a commission that trims the price or a data-centre customer that walks (the Wisconsin plants exist for Microsoft's and Vantage's campuses) leaves the developer holding a permitted site and turbines with no buyer.

**Storage is not disclosed, so it cannot be sold.** No supplier, no per-project list, no ISO totals. A buyer of Invenergy's batteries would be buying a fleet the seller has never described; a supplier selling to it has no named procurement counterpart until 2026's new EVP of Renewable Engineering and Procurement.

**Three owners, one managing member.** The structure works while CDPQ, Blackstone and management want the same thing. A sale of either institution's stake — nothing in the record says one is coming — would trigger every {{change of control}} clause in USD 1.5 billion of revolver and a decade of project debt.

cards.q: A developer is ranked #2 in the US by pipeline and calls itself the 'largest privately held' developer. Are both true?
cards.a: Yes, on different measures. The ranking is development-pipeline megawatts, where NextEra (a utility-owned developer) is first; among developers that are not utilities or public companies, the #2 is the largest — but that is the company's own phrase, not a published ranking.

cards.q: CDPQ holds 52.4 per cent economic ownership of Invenergy Renewables, yet Invenergy management runs it. How?
cards.a: Economic ownership is the right to profits; the managing member of the LLC holds operating control. The pension fund bought cash flow and left control with the founders.

cards.q: What does a build-and-transfer gas plant sell, and to whom?
cards.a: A permitted, constructed plant sold to a regulated utility at commissioning, approved by the commission into rate base under a CPCN. The developer is paid once and exits; the utility's customers pay for forty years.

cards.q: Why would a developer build an 800-mile HVDC line it does not need to sell its existing projects?
cards.a: Because the line creates connection points the queue would never grant, and every generator at its origin is both a line customer and a project the same developer can build. Owning the wire is owning the site rights.

cards.q: A merchant transmission line and a utility transmission line: who pays for each?
cards.a: A merchant line is paid by customers who buy capacity under a FERC open-access tariff; a utility line is paid by all ratepayers through the regulated rate base. The merchant line must find its customers before it can be financed.

cards.q: The DOE terminated a USD 4.9 billion conditional commitment. Did the project lose a loan?
cards.a: It lost a guarantee that had not closed. A conditional commitment is a promise to lend once conditions are met; until closing it can be withdrawn, and this one was, leaving the line to private financing at a higher cost.

cards.q: Interior refunded USD 765 million for four offshore leases. Was the developer made whole?
cards.a: For the lease prices, yes — the amounts match what it paid. Not for years of development spend on Leading Light Wind, and the refund came with a condition to invest in conventional energy.

cards.q: What is a farmdown, and why does a developer do it?
cards.a: Selling a majority of a completed project to a long-term owner (WEC Energy Group at Delilah I and Hardin III) while keeping a stake and the operating role. It returns capital to build the next project.

cards.q: An environmental attribute purchase agreement gives the buyer what?
cards.a: The renewable-energy certificates from the project, without the electricity, which is sold to the grid. The buyer gets the clean-energy claim; the project gets a fixed revenue stream.

cards.q: Why does an infrastructure fund want the pipeline ranking to keep rising?
cards.a: Its investors are limited partners who need to see growth in the platform's value; pipeline megawatts are the visible proxy for a private company that publishes no accounts.

items.q: Which measure puts Invenergy second in the United States?
items.why: Cleanview ranks developers by pipeline; Invenergy's 41,328 MW is second to NextEra's 68,229 MW. No operating-capacity ranking places it there.

items.q: In a build-and-transfer gas deal, when is the developer paid?
c: When the commission grants the certificate
At commissioning, when ownership transfers to the utility

c: Its revenue comes from customers buying capacity under a FERC tariff, not from a utility's rate base
items.why: Merchant transmission earns from transmission service agreements under an open-access tariff; the DOE guarantee was terminated and the line is privately financed.

items.q: Who is the managing member of Invenergy's entities?
items.why: Every release says Invenergy management remains managing member; CDPQ and Blackstone hold the majority of the economics.

items.q: Which technology did the June 2026 offshore settlement money go to, per the company?
c: Gas plants in five states and geothermal
items.why: Invenergy said the USD 765 million would fund gas plants in Indiana, Wisconsin, Iowa, Kansas and Missouri and geothermal development.

items.q: Why do developers own the module factory and the operations company?
c: To capture supplier margin and qualify for domestic-content bonuses
items.why: Illuminate USA's modules go onto Invenergy's own Ohio projects; Invenergy Services operates the fleet — margin kept in-house and content that counts toward bonuses.

items.q: What does a conditional commitment from the DOE Loan Programs Office guarantee?
c: Nothing until closing — it can be withdrawn
items.why: Grain Belt's USD 4.9 billion commitment was conditional; DOE terminated it in July 2025 before closing.
